  "passage_text": "The principal characters in the Republic are Cephalus, Polemarchus,\nThrasymachus, Socrates, Glaucon, and Adeimantus. Cephalus appears in\nthe introduction only, Polemarchus drops at the end of the first\nargument, and Thrasymachus is reduced to silence at the close of the\nfirst book. The main discussion is carried on by Socrates, Glaucon, and\nAdeimantus. Among the company are Lysias (the orator) and Euthydemus,\nthe sons of Cephalus and brothers of Polemarchus, an unknown\nCharmantides—these are mute auditors; also there is Cleitophon, who\nonce interrupts, where, as in the Dialogue which bears his name, he\nappears as the friend and ally of Thrasymachus.\n\nCephalus, the patriarch of the house, has been appropriately engaged in\noffering a sacrifice. He is the pattern of an old man who has almost\ndone with life, and is at peace with himself and with all mankind. He\nfeels that he is drawing nearer to the world below, and seems to linger\naround the memory of the past. He is eager that Socrates should come to\nvisit him, fond of the poetry of the last generation, happy in the\nconsciousness of a well-spent life, glad at having escaped from the\ntyranny of youthful lusts. His love of conversation, his affection, his\nindifference to riches, even his garrulity, are interesting traits of\ncharacter. He is not one of those who have nothing to say, because\ntheir whole mind has been absorbed in making money. Yet he acknowledges\nthat riches have the advantage of placing men above the temptation to\ndishonesty or falsehood. The respectful attention shown to him by\nSocrates, whose love of conversation, no less than the mission imposed\nupon him by the Oracle, leads him to ask questions of all men, young\nand old alike, should also be noted. Who better suited to raise the\nquestion of justice than Cephalus, whose life might seem to be the\nexpression of it? The moderation with which old age is pictured by\nCephalus as a very tolerable portion of existence is characteristic,\nnot only of him, but of Greek feeling generally, and contrasts with the\nexaggeration of Cicero in the De Senectute. The evening of life is\ndescribed by Plato in the most expressive manner, yet with the fewest\npossible touches. As Cicero remarks (Ep. ad Attic. iv. 16), the aged\nCephalus would have been out of place in the discussion which follows,\nand which he could neither have understood nor taken part in without a\nviolation of dramatic propriety (cp. Lysimachus in the Laches).\n\nHis ‘son and heir’ Polemarchus has the frankness and impetuousness of\nyouth; he is for detaining Socrates by force in the opening scene, and\nwill not ‘let him off’ on the subject of women and children. Like\nCephalus, he is limited in his point of view, and represents the\nproverbial stage of morality which has rules of life rather than\nprinciples; and he quotes Simonides (cp. Aristoph. Clouds) as his\nfather had quoted Pindar. But after this he has no more to say; the\nanswers which he makes are only elicited from him by the dialectic of\nSocrates. He has not yet experienced the influence of the Sophists like\nGlaucon and Adeimantus, nor is he sensible of the necessity of refuting\nthem; he belongs to the pre-Socratic or pre-dialectical age. He is\nincapable of arguing, and is bewildered by Socrates to such a degree\nthat he does not know what he is saying. He is made to admit that\njustice is a thief, and that the virtues follow the analogy of the\narts.   "passage_text": "The ‘Chalcedonian giant,’ Thrasymachus, of whom we have already heard\nin the Phaedrus, is the personification of the Sophists, according to\nPlato’s conception of them, in some of their worst characteristics. He\nis vain and blustering, refusing to discourse unless he is paid, fond\nof making an oration, and hoping thereby to escape the inevitable\nSocrates; but a mere child in argument, and unable to foresee that the\nnext ‘move’ (to use a Platonic expression) will ‘shut him up.’ He has\nreached the stage of framing general notions, and in this respect is in\nadvance of Cephalus and Polemarchus. But he is incapable of defending\nthem in a discussion, and vainly tries to cover his confusion with\nbanter and insolence. Whether such doctrines as are attributed to him\nby Plato were really held either by him or by any other Sophist is\nuncertain; in the infancy of philosophy serious errors about morality\nmight easily grow up—they are certainly put into the mouths of speakers\nin Thucydides; but we are concerned at present with Plato’s description\nof him, and not with the historical reality. The inequality of the\ncontest adds greatly to the humour of the scene. The pompous and empty\nSophist is utterly helpless in the hands of the great master of\ndialectic, who knows how to touch all the springs of vanity and\nweakness in him. He is greatly irritated by the irony of Socrates, but\nhis noisy and imbecile rage only lays him more and more open to the\nthrusts of his assailant. His determination to cram down their throats,\nor put ‘bodily into their souls’ his own words, elicits a cry of horror\nfrom Socrates. The state of his temper is quite as worthy of remark as\nthe process of the argument. Nothing is more amusing than his complete\nsubmission when he has been once thoroughly beaten. At first he seems\nto continue the discussion with reluctance, but soon with apparent\ngood-will, and he even testifies his interest at a later stage by one\nor two occasional remarks. When attacked by Glaucon he is humorously\nprotected by Socrates ‘as one who has never been his enemy and is now\nhis friend.’ From Cicero and Quintilian and from Aristotle’s Rhetoric\nwe learn that the Sophist whom Plato has made so ridiculous was a man\nof note whose writings were preserved in later ages. The play on his\nname which was made by his contemporary Herodicus (Aris. Rhet.), ‘thou\nwast ever bold in battle,’ seems to show that the description of him is\nnot devoid of verisimilitude."

But on a nearer\nexamination of them the similarity vanishes, and they are seen to be\ndistinct characters. Glaucon is the impetuous youth who can ‘just never\nhave enough of fechting’ (cp. the character of him in Xen. Mem. iii.\n6); the man of pleasure who is acquainted with the mysteries of love;\nthe ‘juvenis qui gaudet canibus,’ and who improves the breed of\nanimals; the lover of art and music who has all the experiences of\nyouthful life. He is full of quickness and penetration, piercing easily\nbelow the clumsy platitudes of Thrasymachus to the real difficulty; he\nturns out to the light the seamy side of human life, and yet does not\nlose faith in the just and true. It is Glaucon who seizes what may be\ntermed the ludicrous relation of the philosopher to the world, to whom\na state of simplicity is ‘a city of pigs,’ who is always prepared with\na jest when the argument offers him an opportunity, and who is ever\nready to second the humour of Socrates and to appreciate the\nridiculous, whether in the connoisseurs of music, or in the lovers of\ntheatricals, or in the fantastic behaviour of the citizens of\ndemocracy. It is Adeimantus who is the respondent in the more\nargumentative, as Glaucon in the lighter and more imaginative portions\nof the Dialogue. For example, throughout the greater part of the sixth\nbook, the causes of the corruption of philosophy and the conception of\nthe idea of good are discussed with Adeimantus. Glaucon resumes his\nplace of principal respondent; but he has a difficulty in apprehending\nthe higher education of Socrates, and makes some false hits in the\ncourse of the discussion. Once more Adeimantus returns with the\nallusion to his brother Glaucon whom he compares to the contentious\nState; in the next book he is again superseded, and Glaucon continues\nto the end.\n\nThus in a succession of characters Plato represents the successive\nstages of morality, beginning with the Athenian gentleman of the olden\ntime, who is followed by the practical man of that day regulating his\nlife by proverbs and saws; to him succeeds the wild generalization of\nthe Sophists, and lastly come the young disciples of the great teacher,\nwho know the sophistical arguments but will not be convinced by them,\nand desire to go deeper into the nature of things. These too, like\nCephalus, Polemarchus, Thrasymachus, are clearly distinguished from one\nanother. Neither in the Republic, nor in any other Dialogue of Plato,\nis a single character repeated."
}

  "passage_text": "The delineation of Socrates in the Republic is not wholly consistent.
In the first book we have more of the real Socrates, such as he is
depicted in the Memorabilia of Xenophon, in the earliest Dialogues of
Plato, and in the Apology. He is ironical, provoking, questioning, the
old enemy of the Sophists, ready to put on the mask of Silenus as well
as to argue seriously. But in the sixth book his enmity towards the
Sophists abates; he acknowledges that they are the representatives
rather than the corrupters of the world. He also becomes more dogmatic
and constructive, passing beyond the range either of the political or
the speculative ideas of the real Socrates. In one passage Plato
himself seems to intimate that the time had now come for Socrates, who
had passed his whole life in philosophy, to give his own opinion and
not to be always repeating the notions of other men. There is no
evidence that either the idea of good or the conception of a perfect
state were comprehended in the Socratic teaching, though he certainly
dwelt on the nature of the universal and of final causes (cp. Xen.
Mem.; Phaedo); and a deep thinker like him, in his thirty or forty
years of public teaching, could hardly have failed to touch on the
nature of family relations, for which there is also some positive
evidence in the Memorabilia (Mem.) The Socratic method is nominally
retained; and every inference is either put into the mouth of the
respondent or represented as the common discovery of him and Socrates.
But any one can see that this is a mere form, of which the affectation
grows wearisome as the work advances. The method of enquiry has passed
into a method of teaching in which by the help of interlocutors the
same thesis is looked at from various points of view. The nature of the
process is truly characterized by Glaucon, when he describes himself as
a companion who is not good for much in an investigation, but can see
what he is shown, and may, perhaps, give the answer to a question more
fluently than another.

Neither can we be absolutely certain that Socrates himself taught the
immortality of the soul, which is unknown to his disciple Glaucon in
the Republic (cp. Apol.); nor is there any reason to suppose that he
used myths or revelations of another world as a vehicle of instruction,
or that he would have banished poetry or have denounced the Greek
mythology. His favorite oath is retained, and a slight mention is made
of the daemonium, or internal sign, which is alluded to by Socrates as
a phenomenon peculiar to himself. A real element of Socratic teaching,
which is more prominent in the Republic than in any of the other
Dialogues of Plato, is the use of example and illustration τὰ φορτικὰ
αὐτῷ προσφέροντες, ‘Let us apply the test of common instances.’ ‘You,’
says Adeimantus, ironically, in the sixth book, ‘are so unaccustomed to
speak in images.’ And this use of examples or images, though truly
Socratic in origin, is enlarged by the genius of Plato into the form of
an allegory or parable, which embodies in the concrete what has been
already described, or is about to be described, in the abstract. Thus
the figure of the cave in Book VII is a recapitulation of the divisions
of knowledge in Book VI. The composite animal in Book IX is an allegory
of the parts of the soul. The noble captain and the ship and the true
pilot in Book VI are a figure of the relation of the people to the
philosophers in the State which has been described. Other figures, such
as the dog, or the marriage of the portionless maiden, or the drones
and wasps in the eighth and ninth books, also form links of connexion
in long passages, or are used to recall previous discussions.

Plato is most true to the character of his master when he describes him
as ‘not of this world.’ And with this representation of him the ideal
state and the other paradoxes of the Republic are quite in accordance,
though they cannot be shown to have been speculations of Socrates. To
him, as to other great teachers both philosophical and religious, when
they looked upward, the world seemed to be the embodiment of error and
evil. The common sense of mankind has revolted against this view, or
has only partially admitted it. And even in Socrates himself the
sterner judgement of the multitude at times passes into a sort of
ironical pity or love. Men in general are incapable of philosophy, and
are therefore at enmity with the philosopher; but their
misunderstanding of him is unavoidable: for they have never seen him as
he truly is in his own image; they are only acquainted with artificial
systems possessing no native force of truth—words which admit of many
applications. Their leaders have nothing to measure with, and are
therefore ignorant of their own stature. But they are to be pitied or
laughed at, not to be quarrelled with; they mean well with their
nostrums, if they could only learn that they are cutting off a Hydra’s
head. This moderation towards those who are in error is one of the most
characteristic features of Socrates in the Republic. In all the
different representations of Socrates, whether of Xenophon or Plato,
and amid the differences of the earlier or later Dialogues, he always
retains the character of the unwearied and disinterested seeker after
truth, without which he would have ceased to be Socrates.

Leaving the characters we may now analyse the contents of the Republic,
and then proceed to consider (1) The general aspects of this Hellenic
ideal of the State, (2) The modern lights in which the thoughts of
Plato may be read.

BOOK I. The Republic opens with a truly Greek scene—a festival in
honour of the goddess Bendis which is held in the Piraeus; to this is
added the promise of an equestrian torch-race in the evening. The whole
work is supposed to be recited by Socrates on the day after the
festival to a small party, consisting of Critias, Timaeus, Hermocrates,
and another; this we learn from the first words of the Timaeus."

  "passage_text": "When the rhetorical advantage of reciting the Dialogue has been gained,
the attention is not distracted by any reference to the audience; nor
is the reader further reminded of the extraordinary length of the
narrative. Of the numerous company, three only take any serious part in
the discussion; nor are we informed whether in the evening they went to
the torch-race, or talked, as in the Symposium, through the night. The
manner in which the conversation has arisen is described as
follows:—Socrates and his companion Glaucon are about to leave the
festival when they are detained by a message from Polemarchus, who
speedily appears accompanied by Adeimantus, the brother of Glaucon, and
with playful violence compels them to remain, promising them not only
the torch-race, but the pleasure of conversation with the young, which
to Socrates is a far greater attraction. They return to the house of
Cephalus, Polemarchus’ father, now in extreme old age, who is found
sitting upon a cushioned seat crowned for a sacrifice. ‘You should come
to me oftener, Socrates, for I am too old to go to you; and at my time
of life, having lost other pleasures, I care the more for
conversation.’ Socrates asks him what he thinks of age, to which the
old man replies, that the sorrows and discontents of age are to be
attributed to the tempers of men, and that age is a time of peace in
which the tyranny of the passions is no longer felt. Yes, replies
Socrates, but the world will say, Cephalus, that you are happy in old
age because you are rich. ‘And there is something in what they say,
Socrates, but not so much as they imagine—as Themistocles replied to
the Seriphian, “Neither you, if you had been an Athenian, nor I, if I
had been a Seriphian, would ever have been famous,” I might in like
manner reply to you, Neither a good poor man can be happy in age, nor
yet a bad rich man.’ Socrates remarks that Cephalus appears not to care
about riches, a quality which he ascribes to his having inherited, not
acquired them, and would like to know what he considers to be the chief
advantage of them. Cephalus answers that when you are old the belief in
the world below grows upon you, and then to have done justice and never
to have been compelled to do injustice through poverty, and never to
have deceived anyone, are felt to be unspeakable blessings. Socrates,
who is evidently preparing for an argument, next asks, What is the
meaning of the word justice? To tell the truth and pay your debts? No
more than this? Or must we admit exceptions? Ought I, for example, to
put back into the hands of my friend, who has gone mad, the sword which
I borrowed of him when he was in his right mind? ‘There must be
exceptions.’ ‘And yet,’ says Polemarchus, ‘the definition which has
been given has the authority of Simonides.’ Here Cephalus retires to
look after the sacrifices, and bequeaths, as Socrates facetiously
remarks, the possession of the argument to his heir, Polemarchus...

The description of old age is finished, and Plato, as his manner is,
has touched the key-note of the whole work in asking for the definition
of justice, first suggesting the question which Glaucon afterwards
pursues respecting external goods, and preparing for the concluding
mythus of the world below in the slight allusion of Cephalus. The
portrait of the just man is a natural frontispiece or introduction to
the long discourse which follows, and may perhaps imply that in all our
perplexity about the nature of justice, there is no difficulty in
discerning ‘who is a just man.’ The first explanation has been
supported by a saying of Simonides; and now Socrates has a mind to show
that the resolution of justice into two unconnected precepts, which
have no common principle, fails to satisfy the demands of dialectic.

...He proceeds: What did Simonides mean by this saying of his? Did he
mean that I was to give back arms to a madman? ‘No, not in that case,
not if the parties are friends, and evil would result. He meant that
you were to do what was proper, good to friends and harm to enemies.’
Every act does something to somebody; and following this analogy,
Socrates asks, What is this due and proper thing which justice does,
and to whom? He is answered that justice does good to friends and harm
to enemies. But in what way good or harm? ‘In making alliances with the
one, and going to war with the other.’ Then in time of peace what is
the good of justice? The answer is that justice is of use in contracts,
and contracts are money partnerships. Yes; but how in such partnerships
is the just man of more use than any other man? ‘When you want to have
money safely kept and not used.’ Then justice will be useful when money
is useless. And there is another difficulty: justice, like the art of
war or any other art, must be of opposites, good at attack as well as
at defence, at stealing as well as at guarding. But then justice is a
thief, though a hero notwithstanding, like Autolycus, the Homeric hero,
who was ‘excellent above all men in theft and perjury’—to such a pass
have you and Homer and Simonides brought us; though I do not forget
that the thieving must be for the good of friends and the harm of
enemies. And still there arises another question: Are friends to be
interpreted as real or seeming; enemies as real or seeming? And are our
friends to be only the good, and our enemies to be the evil? The answer
is, that we must do good to our seeming and real good friends, and evil
to our seeming and real evil enemies—good to the good, evil to the
evil. But ought we to render evil for evil at all, when to do so will
only make men more evil? Can justice produce injustice any more than
the art of horsemanship can make bad horsemen, or heat produce cold?
The final conclusion is, that no sage or poet ever said that the just
return evil for evil; this was a maxim of some rich and mighty man,
Periander, Perdiccas, or Ismenias the Theban (about B.C. 398-381)..."

  "passage_text": "Thus the first stage of aphoristic or unconscious morality is shown to\nbe inadequate to the wants of the age; the authority of the poets is\nset aside, and through the winding mazes of dialectic we make an\napproach to the Christian precept of forgiveness of injuries. Similar\nwords are applied by the Persian mystic poet to the Divine being when\nthe questioning spirit is stirred within him:—‘If because I do evil,\nThou punishest me by evil, what is the difference between Thee and me?’\nIn this both Plato and Kheyam rise above the level of many Christian\n(?) theologians. The first definition of justice easily passes into the\nsecond; for the simple words ‘to speak the truth and pay your debts’ is\nsubstituted the more abstract ‘to do good to your friends and harm to\nyour enemies.’ Either of these explanations gives a sufficient rule of\nlife for plain men, but they both fall short of the precision of\nphilosophy. We may note in passing the antiquity of casuistry, which\nnot only arises out of the conflict of established principles in\nparticular cases, but also out of the effort to attain them, and is\nprior as well as posterior to our fundamental notions of morality. The\n‘interrogation’ of moral ideas; the appeal to the authority of Homer;\nthe conclusion that the maxim, ‘Do good to your friends and harm to\nyour enemies,’ being erroneous, could not have been the word of any\ngreat man, are all of them very characteristic of the Platonic\nSocrates.\n\n...Here Thrasymachus, who has made several attempts to interrupt, but\nhas hitherto been kept in order by the company, takes advantage of a\npause and rushes into the arena, beginning, like a savage animal, with\na roar. ‘Socrates,’ he says, ‘what folly is this?—Why do you agree to\nbe vanquished by one another in a pretended argument?’ He then\nprohibits all the ordinary definitions of justice; to which Socrates\nreplies that he cannot tell how many twelve is, if he is forbidden to\nsay 2 x 6, or 3 x 4, or 6 x 2, or 4 x 3. At first Thrasymachus is\nreluctant to argue; but at length, with a promise of payment on the\npart of the company and of praise from Socrates, he is induced to open\nthe game. ‘Listen,’ he says, ‘my answer is that might is right, justice\nthe interest of the stronger: now praise me.’ Let me understand you\nfirst. Do you mean that because Polydamas the wrestler, who is stronger\nthan we are, finds the eating of beef for his interest, the eating of\nbeef is also for our interest, who are not so strong? Thrasymachus is\nindignant at the illustration, and in pompous words, apparently\nintended to restore dignity to the argument, he explains his meaning to\nbe that the rulers make laws for their own interests. But suppose, says\nSocrates, that the ruler or stronger makes a mistake—then the interest\nof the stronger is not his interest. Thrasymachus is saved from this\nspeedy downfall by his disciple Cleitophon, who introduces the word\n‘thinks;’—not the actual interest of the ruler, but what he thinks or\nwhat seems to be his interest, is justice. The contradiction is escaped\nby the unmeaning evasion: for though his real and apparent interests\nmay differ, what the ruler thinks to be his interest will always remain\nwhat he thinks to be his interest.\n\nOf course this was not the original assertion, nor is the new\ninterpretation accepted by Thrasymachus himself. But Socrates is not\ndisposed to quarrel about words, if, as he significantly insinuates,\nhis adversary has changed his mind. In what follows Thrasymachus does\nin fact withdraw his admission that the ruler may make a mistake, for\nhe affirms that the ruler as a ruler is infallible. Socrates is quite\nready to accept the new position, which he equally turns against\nThrasymachus by the help of the analogy of the arts. Every art or\nscience has an interest, but this interest is to be distinguished from\nthe accidental interest of the artist, and is only concerned with the\ngood of the things or persons which come under the art. And justice has\nan interest which is the interest not of the ruler or judge, but of\nthose who come under his sway.\n\nThrasymachus is on the brink of the inevitable conclusion, when he\nmakes a bold diversion. ‘Tell me, Socrates,’ he says, ‘have you a\nnurse?’ What a question! Why do you ask? ‘Because, if you have, she\nneglects you and lets you go about drivelling, and has not even taught\nyou to know the shepherd from the sheep. For you fancy that shepherds\nand rulers never think of their own interest, but only of their sheep\nor subjects, whereas the truth is that they fatten them for their use,\nsheep and subjects alike. And experience proves that in every relation\nof life the just man is the loser and the unjust the gainer, especially\nwhere injustice is on the grand scale, which is quite another thing\nfrom the petty rogueries of swindlers and burglars and robbers of\ntemples. The language of men proves this—our ‘gracious’ and ‘blessed’\ntyrant and the like—all which tends to show (1) that justice is the\ninterest of the stronger; and (2) that injustice is more profitable and\nalso stronger than justice.’"
}

having deluged the company with words, has a mind to escape. But the
others will not let him go, and Socrates adds a humble but earnest
request that he will not desert them at such a crisis of their fate.
‘And what can I do more for you?’ he says; ‘would you have me put the
words bodily into your souls?’ God forbid! replies Socrates; but we
want you to be consistent in the use of terms, and not to employ
‘physician’ in an exact sense, and then again ‘shepherd’ or ‘ruler’ in
an inexact,—if the words are strictly taken, the ruler and the shepherd
look only to the good of their people or flocks and not to their own:
whereas you insist that rulers are solely actuated by love of office.
‘No doubt about it,’ replies Thrasymachus. Then why are they paid? Is
not the reason, that their interest is not comprehended in their art,
and is therefore the concern of another art, the art of pay, which is
common to the arts in general, and therefore not identical with any one
of them? Nor would any man be a ruler unless he were induced by the
hope of reward or the fear of punishment;—the reward is money or
honour, the punishment is the necessity of being ruled by a man worse
than himself. And if a State (or Church) were composed entirely of good
men, they would be affected by the last motive only; and there would be
as much ‘nolo episcopari’ as there is at present of the opposite...

The satire on existing governments is heightened by the simple and
apparently incidental manner in which the last remark is introduced.
There is a similar irony in the argument that the governors of mankind
do not like being in office, and that therefore they demand pay.

...Enough of this: the other assertion of Thrasymachus is far more
important—that the unjust life is more gainful than the just. Now, as
you and I, Glaucon, are not convinced by him, we must reply to him; but
if we try to compare their respective gains we shall want a judge to
decide for us; we had better therefore proceed by making mutual
admissions of the truth to one another.

Thrasymachus had asserted that perfect injustice was more gainful than
perfect justice, and after a little hesitation he is induced by
Socrates to admit the still greater paradox that injustice is virtue
and justice vice. Socrates praises his frankness, and assumes the
attitude of one whose only wish is to understand the meaning of his
opponents. At the same time he is weaving a net in which Thrasymachus
is finally enclosed. The admission is elicited from him that the just
man seeks to gain an advantage over the unjust only, but not over the
just, while the unjust would gain an advantage over either. Socrates,
in order to test this statement, employs once more the favourite
analogy of the arts. The musician, doctor, skilled artist of any sort,
does not seek to gain more than the skilled, but only more than the
unskilled (that is to say, he works up to a rule, standard, law, and
does not exceed it), whereas the unskilled makes random efforts at
excess. Thus the skilled falls on the side of the good, and the
unskilled on the side of the evil, and the just is the skilled, and the
unjust is the unskilled.

There was great difficulty in bringing Thrasymachus to the point; the
day was hot and he was streaming with perspiration, and for the first
time in his life he was seen to blush. But his other thesis that
injustice was stronger than justice has not yet been refuted, and
Socrates now proceeds to the consideration of this, which, with the
assistance of Thrasymachus, he hopes to clear up; the latter is at
first churlish, but in the judicious hands of Socrates is soon restored
to good-humour: Is there not honour among thieves? Is not the strength
of injustice only a remnant of justice? Is not absolute injustice
absolute weakness also? A house that is divided against itself cannot
stand; two men who quarrel detract from one another’s strength, and he
who is at war with himself is the enemy of himself and the gods. Not
wickedness therefore, but semi-wickedness flourishes in states,—a
remnant of good is needed in order to make union in action
possible,—there is no kingdom of evil in this world.

Another question has not been answered: Is the just or the unjust the
happier? To this we reply, that every art has an end and an excellence
or virtue by which the end is accomplished. And is not the end of the
soul happiness, and justice the excellence of the soul by which
happiness is attained? Justice and happiness being thus shown to be
inseparable, the question whether the just or the unjust is the happier
has disappeared.

Thrasymachus replies: ‘Let this be your entertainment, Socrates, at the
festival of Bendis.’ Yes; and a very good entertainment with which your
kindness has supplied me, now that you have left off scolding. And yet
not a good entertainment—but that was my own fault, for I tasted of too
many things. First of all the nature of justice was the subject of our
enquiry, and then whether justice is virtue and wisdom, or evil and
folly; and then the comparative advantages of just and unjust: and the
sum of all is that I know not what justice is; how then shall I know
whether the just is happy or not?..."

  "passage_text": "Thus the sophistical fabric has been demolished, chiefly by appealing
to the analogy of the arts. ‘Justice is like the arts (1) in having no
external interest, and (2) in not aiming at excess, and (3) justice is
to happiness what the implement of the workman is to his work.’ At this
the modern reader is apt to stumble, because he forgets that Plato is
writing in an age when the arts and the virtues, like the moral and
intellectual faculties, were still undistinguished. Among early
enquirers into the nature of human action the arts helped to fill up
the void of speculation; and at first the comparison of the arts and
the virtues was not perceived by them to be fallacious. They only saw
the points of agreement in them and not the points of difference.
Virtue, like art, must take means to an end; good manners are both an
art and a virtue; character is naturally described under the image of a
statue; and there are many other figures of speech which are readily
transferred from art to morals. The next generation cleared up these
perplexities; or at least supplied after ages with a further analysis
of them. The contemporaries of Plato were in a state of transition, and
had not yet fully realized the common-sense distinction of Aristotle,
that ‘virtue is concerned with action, art with production’ (Nic.
Eth.), or that ‘virtue implies intention and constancy of purpose,’
whereas ‘art requires knowledge only’. And yet in the absurdities which
follow from some uses of the analogy, there seems to be an intimation
conveyed that virtue is more than art. This is implied in the reductio
ad absurdum that ‘justice is a thief,’ and in the dissatisfaction which
Socrates expresses at the final result.

The expression ‘an art of pay’ which is described as ‘common to all the
arts’ is not in accordance with the ordinary use of language. Nor is it
employed elsewhere either by Plato or by any other Greek writer. It is
suggested by the argument, and seems to extend the conception of art to
doing as well as making. Another flaw or inaccuracy of language may be
noted in the words ‘men who are injured are made more unjust.’ For
those who are injured are not necessarily made worse, but only harmed
or ill-treated.

The second of the three arguments, ‘that the just does not aim at
excess,’ has a real meaning, though wrapped up in an enigmatical form.
That the good is of the nature of the finite is a peculiarly Hellenic
sentiment, which may be compared with the language of those modern
writers who speak of virtue as fitness, and of freedom as obedience to
law. The mathematical or logical notion of limit easily passes into an
ethical one, and even finds a mythological expression in the conception
of envy (Greek). Ideas of measure, equality, order, unity, proportion,
still linger in the writings of moralists; and the true spirit of the
fine arts is better conveyed by such terms than by superlatives.

‘When workmen strive to do better than well,
They do confound their skill in covetousness.’ (King John. Act. iv. Sc.
2.)

The harmony of the soul and body, and of the parts of the soul with one
another, a harmony ‘fairer than that of musical notes,’ is the true
Hellenic mode of conceiving the perfection of human nature.

In what may be called the epilogue of the discussion with Thrasymachus,
Plato argues that evil is not a principle of strength, but of discord
and dissolution, just touching the question which has been often
treated in modern times by theologians and philosophers, of the
negative nature of evil. In the last argument we trace the germ of the
Aristotelian doctrine of an end and a virtue directed towards the end,
which again is suggested by the arts. The final reconcilement of
justice and happiness and the identity of the individual and the State
are also intimated. Socrates reassumes the character of a
‘know-nothing;’ at the same time he appears to be not wholly satisfied
with the manner in which the argument has been conducted. Nothing is
concluded; but the tendency of the dialectical process, here as always,
is to enlarge our conception of ideas, and to widen their application
to human life.

BOOK II. Thrasymachus is pacified, but the intrepid Glaucon insists on
continuing the argument. He is not satisfied with the indirect manner
in which, at the end of the last book, Socrates had disposed of the
question ‘Whether the just or the unjust is the happier.’ He begins by
dividing goods into three classes:—first, goods desirable in
themselves; secondly, goods desirable in themselves and for their
results; thirdly, goods desirable for their results only. He then asks
Socrates in which of the three classes he would place justice. In the
second class, replies Socrates, among goods desirable for themselves
and also for their results. ‘Then the world in general are of another
mind, for they say that justice belongs to the troublesome class of
goods which are desirable for their results only. Socrates answers that
this is the doctrine of Thrasymachus which he rejects. Glaucon thinks
that Thrasymachus was too ready to listen to the voice of the charmer,
and proposes to consider the nature of justice and injustice in
themselves and apart from the results and rewards of them which the
world is always dinning in his ears. He will first of all speak of the
nature and origin of justice; secondly, of the manner in which men view
justice as a necessity and not a good; and thirdly, he will prove the
reasonableness of this view."

  "passage_text": "‘To do injustice is said to be a good; to suffer injustice an evil. As
the evil is discovered by experience to be greater than the good, the
sufferers, who cannot also be doers, make a compact that they will have
neither, and this compact or mean is called justice, but is really the
impossibility of doing injustice. No one would observe such a compact
if he were not obliged. Let us suppose that the just and unjust have
two rings, like that of Gyges in the well-known story, which make them
invisible, and then no difference will appear in them, for every one
will do evil if he can. And he who abstains will be regarded by the
world as a fool for his pains. Men may praise him in public out of fear
for themselves, but they will laugh at him in their hearts (Cp.
Gorgias.)

‘And now let us frame an ideal of the just and unjust. Imagine the
unjust man to be master of his craft, seldom making mistakes and easily
correcting them; having gifts of money, speech, strength—the greatest
villain bearing the highest character: and at his side let us place the
just in his nobleness and simplicity—being, not seeming—without name or
reward—clothed in his justice only—the best of men who is thought to be
the worst, and let him die as he has lived. I might add (but I would
rather put the rest into the mouth of the panegyrists of injustice—they
will tell you) that the just man will be scourged, racked, bound, will
have his eyes put out, and will at last be crucified (literally
impaled)—and all this because he ought to have preferred seeming to
being. How different is the case of the unjust who clings to appearance
as the true reality! His high character makes him a ruler; he can marry
where he likes, trade where he likes, help his friends and hurt his
enemies; having got rich by dishonesty he can worship the gods better,
and will therefore be more loved by them than the just.’

I was thinking what to answer, when Adeimantus joined in the already
unequal fray. He considered that the most important point of all had
been omitted:—‘Men are taught to be just for the sake of rewards;
parents and guardians make reputation the incentive to virtue. And
other advantages are promised by them of a more solid kind, such as
wealthy marriages and high offices. There are the pictures in Homer and
Hesiod of fat sheep and heavy fleeces, rich corn-fields and trees
toppling with fruit, which the gods provide in this life for the just.
And the Orphic poets add a similar picture of another. The heroes of
Musaeus and Eumolpus lie on couches at a festival, with garlands on
their heads, enjoying as the meed of virtue a paradise of immortal
drunkenness. Some go further, and speak of a fair posterity in the
third and fourth generation. But the wicked they bury in a slough and
make them carry water in a sieve: and in this life they attribute to
them the infamy which Glaucon was assuming to be the lot of the just
who are supposed to be unjust.

prose:—“Virtue,” as Hesiod says, “is honourable but difficult, vice is
easy and profitable.” You may often see the wicked in great prosperity
and the righteous afflicted by the will of heaven. And mendicant
prophets knock at rich men’s doors, promising to atone for the sins of
themselves or their fathers in an easy fashion with sacrifices and
festive games, or with charms and invocations to get rid of an enemy
good or bad by divine help and at a small charge;—they appeal to books
professing to be written by Musaeus and Orpheus, and carry away the
minds of whole cities, and promise to “get souls out of purgatory;” and
if we refuse to listen to them, no one knows what will happen to us.

‘When a lively-minded ingenuous youth hears all this, what will be his
conclusion? “Will he,” in the language of Pindar, “make justice his
high tower, or fortify himself with crooked deceit?” Justice, he
reflects, without the appearance of justice, is misery and ruin;
injustice has the promise of a glorious life. Appearance is master of
truth and lord of happiness. To appearance then I will turn,—I will put
on the show of virtue and trail behind me the fox of Archilochus. I
hear some one saying that “wickedness is not easily concealed,” to
which I reply that “nothing great is easy.” Union and force and
rhetoric will do much; and if men say that they cannot prevail over the
gods, still how do we know that there are gods? Only from the poets,
who acknowledge that they may be appeased by sacrifices. Then why not
sin and pay for indulgences out of your sin? For if the righteous are
only unpunished, still they have no further reward, while the wicked
may be unpunished and have the pleasure of sinning too. But what of the
world below? Nay, says the argument, there are atoning powers who will
set that matter right, as the poets, who are the sons of the gods, tell
us; and this is confirmed by the authority of the State.

‘How can we resist such arguments in favour of injustice? Add good
manners, and, as the wise tell us, we shall make the best of both
worlds. Who that is not a miserable caitiff will refrain from smiling
at the praises of justice? Even if a man knows the better part he will
not be angry with others; for he knows also that more than human virtue
is needed to save a man, and that he only praises justice who is
incapable of injustice."
}

Had we been taught\nin early youth the power of justice and injustice inherent in the soul,\nand unseen by any human or divine eye, we should not have needed others\nto be our guardians, but every one would have been the guardian of\nhimself. This is what I want you to show, Socrates;—other men use\narguments which rather tend to strengthen the position of Thrasymachus\nthat “might is right;” but from you I expect better things. And please,\nas Glaucon said, to exclude reputation; let the just be thought unjust\nand the unjust just, and do you still prove to us the superiority of\njustice’...\n\nThe thesis, which for the sake of argument has been maintained by\nGlaucon, is the converse of that of Thrasymachus—not right is the\ninterest of the stronger, but right is the necessity of the weaker.\nStarting from the same premises he carries the analysis of society a\nstep further back;—might is still right, but the might is the weakness\nof the many combined against the strength of the few.\n\nThere have been theories in modern as well as in ancient times which\nhave a family likeness to the speculations of Glaucon; e.g. that power\nis the foundation of right; or that a monarch has a divine right to\ngovern well or ill; or that virtue is self-love or the love of power;\nor that war is the natural state of man; or that private vices are\npublic benefits. All such theories have a kind of plausibility from\ntheir partial agreement with experience. For human nature oscillates\nbetween good and evil, and the motives of actions and the origin of\ninstitutions may be explained to a certain extent on either hypothesis\naccording to the character or point of view of a particular thinker.\nThe obligation of maintaining authority under all circumstances and\nsometimes by rather questionable means is felt strongly and has become\na sort of instinct among civilized men. The divine right of kings, or\nmore generally of governments, is one of the forms under which this\nnatural feeling is expressed. Nor again is there any evil which has not\nsome accompaniment of good or pleasure; nor any good which is free from\nsome alloy of evil; nor any noble or generous thought which may not be\nattended by a shadow or the ghost of a shadow of self-interest or of\nself-love. We know that all human actions are imperfect; but we do not\ntherefore attribute them to the worse rather than to the better motive\nor principle. Such a philosophy is both foolish and false, like that\nopinion of the clever rogue who assumes all other men to be like\nhimself. And theories of this sort do not represent the real nature of\nthe State, which is based on a vague sense of right gradually corrected\nand enlarged by custom and law (although capable also of perversion),\nany more than they describe the origin of society, which is to be\nsought in the family and in the social and religious feelings of man.\nNor do they represent the average character of individuals, which\ncannot be explained simply on a theory of evil, but has always a\ncounteracting element of good. And as men become better such theories\nappear more and more untruthful to them, because they are more\nconscious of their own disinterestedness. A little experience may make\na man a cynic; a great deal will bring him back to a truer and kindlier\nview of the mixed nature of himself and his fellow men.\n\nThe two brothers ask Socrates to prove to them that the just is happy\nwhen they have taken from him all that in which happiness is ordinarily\nsupposed to consist. Not that there is (1) any absurdity in the attempt\nto frame a notion of justice apart from circumstances. For the ideal\nmust always be a paradox when compared with the ordinary conditions of\nhuman life. Neither the Stoical ideal nor the Christian ideal is true\nas a fact, but they may serve as a basis of education, and may exercise\nan ennobling influence. An ideal is none the worse because ‘some one\nhas made the discovery’ that no such ideal was ever realized. And in a\nfew exceptional individuals who are raised above the ordinary level of\nhumanity, the ideal of happiness may be realized in death and misery.\nThis may be the state which the reason deliberately approves, and which\nthe utilitarian as well as every other moralist may be bound in certain\ncases to prefer.\n\nNor again, (2) must we forget that Plato, though he agrees generally\nwith the view implied in the argument of the two brothers, is not\nexpressing his own final conclusion, but rather seeking to dramatize\none of the aspects of ethical truth. He is developing his idea\ngradually in a series of positions or situations. He is exhibiting\nSocrates for the first time undergoing the Socratic interrogation.\nLastly, (3) the word ‘happiness’ involves some degree of confusion\nbecause associated in the language of modern philosophy with conscious\npleasure or satisfaction, which was not equally present to his mind."

  "passage_text": "Glaucon has been drawing a picture of the misery of the just and the
happiness of the unjust, to which the misery of the tyrant in Book IX
is the answer and parallel. And still the unjust must appear just; that
is ‘the homage which vice pays to virtue.’ But now Adeimantus, taking
up the hint which had been already given by Glaucon, proceeds to show
that in the opinion of mankind justice is regarded only for the sake of
rewards and reputation, and points out the advantage which is given to
such arguments as those of Thrasymachus and Glaucon by the conventional
morality of mankind. He seems to feel the difficulty of ‘justifying the
ways of God to man.’ Both the brothers touch upon the question, whether
the morality of actions is determined by their consequences; and both
of them go beyond the position of Socrates, that justice belongs to the
class of goods not desirable for themselves only, but desirable for
themselves and for their results, to which he recalls them. In their
attempt to view justice as an internal principle, and in their
condemnation of the poets, they anticipate him. The common life of
Greece is not enough for them; they must penetrate deeper into the
nature of things.

It has been objected that justice is honesty in the sense of Glaucon
and Adeimantus, but is taken by Socrates to mean all virtue. May we not
more truly say that the old-fashioned notion of justice is enlarged by
Socrates, and becomes equivalent to universal order or well-being,
first in the State, and secondly in the individual? He has found a new
answer to his old question (Protag.), ‘whether the virtues are one or
many,’ viz. that one is the ordering principle of the three others. In
seeking to establish the purely internal nature of justice, he is met
by the fact that man is a social being, and he tries to harmonise the
two opposite theses as well as he can. There is no more inconsistency
in this than was inevitable in his age and country; there is no use in
turning upon him the cross lights of modern philosophy, which, from
some other point of view, would appear equally inconsistent. Plato does
not give the final solution of philosophical questions for us; nor can
he be judged of by our standard.

The remainder of the Republic is developed out of the question of the
sons of Ariston. Three points are deserving of remark in what
immediately follows:—First, that the answer of Socrates is altogether
indirect. He does not say that happiness consists in the contemplation
of the idea of justice, and still less will he be tempted to affirm the
Stoical paradox that the just man can be happy on the rack. But first
he dwells on the difficulty of the problem and insists on restoring man
to his natural condition, before he will answer the question at all. He
too will frame an ideal, but his ideal comprehends not only abstract
justice, but the whole relations of man. Under the fanciful
illustration of the large letters he implies that he will only look for
justice in society, and that from the State he will proceed to the
individual. His answer in substance amounts to this,—that under
favourable conditions, i.e. in the perfect State, justice and happiness
will coincide, and that when justice has been once found, happiness may
be left to take care of itself. That he falls into some degree of
inconsistency, when in the tenth book he claims to have got rid of the
rewards and honours of justice, may be admitted; for he has left those
which exist in the perfect State. And the philosopher ‘who retires
under the shelter of a wall’ can hardly have been esteemed happy by
him, at least not in this world. Still he maintains the true attitude
of moral action. Let a man do his duty first, without asking whether he
will be happy or not, and happiness will be the inseparable accident
which attends him. ‘Seek ye first the kingdom of God and his
righteousness, and all these things shall be added unto you.’

Secondly, it may be remarked that Plato preserves the genuine character
of Greek thought in beginning with the State and in going on to the
individual. First ethics, then politics—this is the order of ideas to
us; the reverse is the order of history. Only after many struggles of
thought does the individual assert his right as a moral being. In early
ages he is not ONE, but one of many, the citizen of a State which is
prior to him; and he has no notion of good or evil apart from the law
of his country or the creed of his church. And to this type he is
constantly tending to revert, whenever the influence of custom, or of
party spirit, or the recollection of the past becomes too strong for
him.

Thirdly, we may observe the confusion or identification of the
individual and the State, of ethics and politics, which pervades early
Greek speculation, and even in modern times retains a certain degree of
influence. The subtle difference between the collective and individual
action of mankind seems to have escaped early thinkers, and we too are
sometimes in danger of forgetting the conditions of united human
action, whenever we either elevate politics into ethics, or lower
ethics to the standard of politics. The good man and the good citizen
only coincide in the perfect State; and this perfection cannot be
attained by legislation acting upon them from without, but, if at all,
by education fashioning them from within."
}

  "passage_text": "...Socrates praises the sons of Ariston, ‘inspired offspring of the\nrenowned hero,’ as the elegiac poet terms them; but he does not\nunderstand how they can argue so eloquently on behalf of injustice\nwhile their character shows that they are uninfluenced by their own\narguments. He knows not how to answer them, although he is afraid of\ndeserting justice in the hour of need. He therefore makes a condition,\nthat having weak eyes he shall be allowed to read the large letters\nfirst and then go on to the smaller, that is, he must look for justice\nin the State first, and will then proceed to the individual.\nAccordingly he begins to construct the State.\n\nSociety arises out of the wants of man. His first want is food; his\nsecond a house; his third a coat. The sense of these needs and the\npossibility of satisfying them by exchange, draw individuals together\non the same spot; and this is the beginning of a State, which we take\nthe liberty to invent, although necessity is the real inventor. There\nmust be first a husbandman, secondly a builder, thirdly a weaver, to\nwhich may be added a cobbler. Four or five citizens at least are\nrequired to make a city. Now men have different natures, and one man\nwill do one thing better than many; and business waits for no man.\nHence there must be a division of labour into different employments;\ninto wholesale and retail trade; into workers, and makers of workmen’s\ntools; into shepherds and husbandmen. A city which includes all this\nwill have far exceeded the limit of four or five, and yet not be very\nlarge. But then again imports will be required, and imports necessitate\nexports, and this implies variety of produce in order to attract the\ntaste of purchasers; also merchants and ships. In the city too we must\nhave a market and money and retail trades; otherwise buyers and sellers\nwill never meet, and the valuable time of the producers will be wasted\nin vain efforts at exchange. If we add hired servants the State will be\ncomplete. And we may guess that somewhere in the intercourse of the\ncitizens with one another justice and injustice will appear.\n\nHere follows a rustic picture of their way of life. They spend their\ndays in houses which they have built for themselves; they make their\nown clothes and produce their own corn and wine. Their principal food\nis meal and flour, and they drink in moderation. They live on the best\nof terms with each other, and take care not to have too many children.\n‘But,’ said Glaucon, interposing, ‘are they not to have a relish?’\nCertainly; they will have salt and olives and cheese, vegetables and\nfruits, and chestnuts to roast at the fire. ‘’Tis a city of pigs,\nSocrates.’ Why, I replied, what do you want more? ‘Only the comforts of\nlife,—sofas and tables, also sauces and sweets.’ I see; you want not\nonly a State, but a luxurious State; and possibly in the more complex\nframe we may sooner find justice and injustice. Then the fine arts must\ngo to work—every conceivable instrument and ornament of luxury will be\nwanted. There will be dancers, painters, sculptors, musicians, cooks,\nbarbers, tire-women, nurses, artists; swineherds and neatherds too for\nthe animals, and physicians to cure the disorders of which luxury is\nthe source. To feed all these superfluous mouths we shall need a part\nof our neighbour’s land, and they will want a part of ours. And this is\nthe origin of war, which may be traced to the same causes as other\npolitical evils. Our city will now require the slight addition of a\ncamp, and the citizen will be converted into a soldier. But then again\nour old doctrine of the division of labour must not be forgotten. The\nart of war cannot be learned in a day, and there must be a natural\naptitude for military duties. There will be some warlike natures who\nhave this aptitude—dogs keen of scent, swift of foot to pursue, and\nstrong of limb to fight. And as spirit is the foundation of courage,\nsuch natures, whether of men or animals, will be full of spirit. But\nthese spirited natures are apt to bite and devour one another; the\nunion of gentleness to friends and fierceness against enemies appears\nto be an impossibility, and the guardian of a State requires both\nqualities. Your\ndog is a philosopher who judges by the rule of knowing or not knowing;\nand philosophy, whether in man or beast, is the parent of gentleness.\nThe human watchdogs must be philosophers or lovers of learning which\nwill make them gentle. And how are they to be learned without\neducation?"

Music\nincludes literature, and literature is of two kinds, true and false.\n‘What do you mean?’ he said. I mean that children hear stories before\nthey learn gymnastics, and that the stories are either untrue, or have\nat most one or two grains of truth in a bushel of falsehood. Now early\nlife is very impressible, and children ought not to learn what they\nwill have to unlearn when they grow up; we must therefore have a\ncensorship of nursery tales, banishing some and keeping others. Some of\nthem are very improper, as we may see in the great instances of Homer\nand Hesiod, who not only tell lies but bad lies; stories about Uranus\nand Saturn, which are immoral as well as false, and which should never\nbe spoken of to young persons, or indeed at all; or, if at all, then in\na mystery, after the sacrifice, not of an Eleusinian pig, but of some\nunprocurable animal. Shall our youth be encouraged to beat their\nfathers by the example of Zeus, or our citizens be incited to quarrel\nby hearing or seeing representations of strife among the gods? Shall\nthey listen to the narrative of Hephaestus binding his mother, and of\nZeus sending him flying for helping her when she was beaten? Such tales\nmay possibly have a mystical interpretation, but the young are\nincapable of understanding allegory. Reason teaches us this; for if we suppose a change\nin God, he must be changed either by another or by himself. By\nanother?—but the best works of nature and art and the noblest qualities\nof mind are least liable to be changed by any external force. By\nhimself?—but he cannot change for the better; he will hardly change for\nthe worse. He remains for ever fairest and best in his own image.\nTherefore we refuse to listen to the poets who tell us of Here begging\nin the likeness of a priestess or of other deities who prowl about at\nnight in strange disguises; all that blasphemous nonsense with which\nmothers fool the manhood out of their children must be suppressed. For they are\nnot ignorant of antiquity like the poets, nor are they afraid of their\nenemies, nor is any madman a friend of theirs. God then is true, he is\nabsolutely true; he changes not, he deceives not, by day or night, by\nword or sign. This is our second great principle—God is true. Away with\nthe lying dream of Agamemnon in Homer, and the accusation of Thetis\nagainst Apollo in Aeschylus...\n\nIn order to give clearness to his conception of the State, Plato\nproceeds to trace the first principles of mutual need and of division\nof labour in an imaginary community of four or five citizens. Gradually\nthis community increases; the division of labour extends to countries;\nimports necessitate exports; a medium of exchange is required, and\nretailers sit in the market-place to save the time of the producers.\nThese are the steps by which Plato constructs the first or primitive\nState, introducing the elements of political economy by the way. The last subject, and also the origin of\nRetail Trade, is treated with admirable lucidity in the second book of\nthe Republic. But Plato never combined his economic ideas into a\nsystem, and never seems to have recognized that Trade is one of the\ngreat motive powers of the State and of the world. He would make retail\ntraders only of the inferior sort of citizens (Rep., Laws), though he\nremarks, quaintly enough (Laws), that ‘if only the best men and the\nbest women everywhere were compelled to keep taverns for a time or to\ncarry on retail trade, etc., then we should knew how pleasant and\nagreeable all these things are.’\n\nThe disappointment of Glaucon at the ‘city of pigs,’ the ludicrous\ndescription of the ministers of luxury in the more refined State, and\nthe afterthought of the necessity of doctors, the illustration of the\nnature of the guardian taken from the dog, the desirableness of\noffering some almost unprocurable victim when impure mysteries are to\nbe celebrated, the behaviour of Zeus to his father and of Hephaestus to\nhis mother, are touches of humour which have also a serious meaning. This is also the substance of Plato’s\nview, though he must be acknowledged to have drawn the line somewhat\ndifferently from modern ethical writers, respecting truth and\nfalsehood. To us, economies or accommodations would not be allowable\nunless they were required by the human faculties or necessary for the\ncommunication of knowledge to the simple and ignorant. We should insist\nthat the word was inseparable from the intention, and that we must not\nbe ‘falsely true,’ i.e. speak or act falsely in support of what was\nright or true. But Plato would limit the use of fictions only by\nrequiring that they should have a good moral effect, and that such a\ndangerous weapon as falsehood should be employed by the rulers alone\nand for great objects.\n\nA Greek in the age of Plato attached no importance to the question\nwhether his religion was an historical fact. He was just beginning to\nbe conscious that the past had a history; but he could see nothing\nbeyond Homer and Hesiod. Whether their narratives were true or false\ndid not seriously affect the political or social life of Hellas. Men\nonly began to suspect that they were fictions when they recognised them\nto be immoral. And so in all religions: the consideration of their\nmorality comes first, afterwards the truth of the documents in which\nthey are recorded, or of the events natural or supernatural which are\ntold of them. We know also\nthat changes in the traditions of a country cannot be made in a day;\nand are therefore tolerant of many things which science and criticism\nwould condemn."

That anachronisms whether of religion or law, when men\nhave reached another stage of civilization, should be got rid of by\nfictions is in accordance with universal experience. Great is the art\nof interpretation; and by a natural process, which when once discovered\nwas always going on, what could not be altered was explained away. And\nso without any palpable inconsistency there existed side by side two\nforms of religion, the tradition inherited or invented by the poets and\nthe customary worship of the temple; on the other hand, there was the\nreligion of the philosopher, who was dwelling in the heaven of ideas,\nbut did not therefore refuse to offer a cock to Aesculapius, or to be\nseen saying his prayers at the rising of the sun. At length the\nantagonism between the popular and philosophical religion, never so\ngreat among the Greeks as in our own age, disappeared, and was only\nfelt like the difference between the religion of the educated and\nuneducated among ourselves.   "passage_text": "BOOK III. There is another motive in purifying religion, which is to\nbanish fear; for no man can be courageous who is afraid of death, or\nwho believes the tales which are repeated by the poets concerning the\nworld below. They must be gently requested not to abuse hell; they may\nbe reminded that their stories are both untrue and discouraging. Nor\nmust they be angry if we expunge obnoxious passages, such as the\ndepressing words of Achilles—‘I would rather be a serving-man than rule\nover all the dead;’ and the verses which tell of the squalid mansions,\nthe senseless shadows, the flitting soul mourning over lost strength\nand youth, the soul with a gibber going beneath the earth like smoke,\nor the souls of the suitors which flutter about like bats. The terrors\nand horrors of Cocytus and Styx, ghosts and sapless shades, and the\nrest of their Tartarean nomenclature, must vanish. Such tales may have\ntheir use; but they are not the proper food for soldiers. As little can\nwe admit the sorrows and sympathies of the Homeric heroes:—Achilles,\nthe son of Thetis, in tears, throwing ashes on his head, or pacing up\nand down the sea-shore in distraction; or Priam, the cousin of the\ngods, crying aloud, rolling in the mire. A good man is not prostrated\nat the loss of children or fortune. Neither is death terrible to him;\nand therefore lamentations over the dead should not be practised by men\nof note; they should be the concern of inferior persons only, whether\nwomen or men. Still worse is the attribution of such weakness to the\ngods; as when the goddesses say, ‘Alas! my travail!’ and worst of all,\nwhen the king of heaven himself laments his inability to save Hector,\nor sorrows over the impending doom of his dear Sarpedon. Such a\ncharacter of God, if not ridiculed by our young men, is likely to be\nimitated by them. Nor should our citizens be given to excess of\nlaughter—‘Such violent delights’ are followed by a violent re-action.\nThe description in the Iliad of the gods shaking their sides at the\nclumsiness of Hephaestus will not be admitted by us. ‘Certainly not.’\n\nTruth should have a high place among the virtues, for falsehood, as we\nwere saying, is useless to the gods, and only useful to men as a\nmedicine. But this employment of falsehood must remain a privilege of\nstate; the common man must not in return tell a lie to the ruler; any\nmore than the patient would tell a lie to his physician, or the sailor\nto his captain.\n\nIn the next place our youth must be temperate, and temperance consists\nin self-control and obedience to authority. That is a lesson which\nHomer teaches in some places: ‘The Achaeans marched on breathing\nprowess, in silent awe of their leaders;’—but a very different one in\nother places: ‘O heavy with wine, who hast the eyes of a dog, but the\nheart of a stag.’ Language of the latter kind will not impress\nself-control on the minds of youth. The same may be said about his\npraises of eating and drinking and his dread of starvation; also about\nthe verses in which he tells of the rapturous loves of Zeus and Here,\nor of how Hephaestus once detained Ares and Aphrodite in a net on a\nsimilar occasion. There is a nobler strain heard in the words:—‘Endure,\nmy soul, thou hast endured worse.’ Nor must we allow our citizens to\nreceive bribes, or to say, ‘Gifts persuade the gods, gifts reverend\nkings;’ or to applaud the ignoble advice of Phoenix to Achilles that he\nshould get money out of the Greeks before he assisted them; or the\nmeanness of Achilles himself in taking gifts from Agamemnon; or his\nrequiring a ransom for the body of Hector; or his cursing of Apollo; or\nhis insolence to the river-god Scamander; or his dedication to the dead\nPatroclus of his own hair which had been already dedicated to the other\nriver-god Spercheius; or his cruelty in dragging the body of Hector\nround the walls, and slaying the captives at the pyre: such a\ncombination of meanness and cruelty in Cheiron’s pupil is\ninconceivable. The amatory exploits of Peirithous and Theseus are\nequally unworthy. Either these so-called sons of gods were not the sons\nof gods, or they were not such as the poets imagine them, any more than\nthe gods themselves are the authors of evil. The youth who believes\nthat such things are done by those who have the blood of heaven flowing\nin their veins will be too ready to imitate their example.\n\nEnough of gods and heroes;—what shall we say about men? What the poets\nand story-tellers say—that the wicked prosper and the righteous are\nafflicted, or that justice is another’s gain? Such misrepresentations\ncannot be allowed by us. But in this we are anticipating the definition\nof justice, and had therefore better defer the enquiry."
}

  "passage_text": "The subjects of poetry have been sufficiently treated; next follows\nstyle. Now all poetry is a narrative of events past, present, or to\ncome; and narrative is of three kinds, the simple, the imitative, and a\ncomposition of the two. An instance will make my meaning clear. The\nfirst scene in Homer is of the last or mixed kind, being partly\ndescription and partly dialogue. But if you throw the dialogue into the\n‘oratio obliqua,’ the passage will run thus: The priest came and prayed\nApollo that the Achaeans might take Troy and have a safe return if\nAgamemnon would only give him back his daughter; and the other Greeks\nassented, but Agamemnon was wroth, and so on—The whole then becomes\ndescriptive, and the poet is the only speaker left; or, if you omit the\nnarrative, the whole becomes dialogue. These are the three styles—which\nof them is to be admitted into our State? ‘Do you ask whether tragedy\nand comedy are to be admitted?’ Yes, but also something more—Is it not\ndoubtful whether our guardians are to be imitators at all? Or rather,\nhas not the question been already answered, for we have decided that\none man cannot in his life play many parts, any more than he can act\nboth tragedy and comedy, or be rhapsodist and actor at once? Human\nnature is coined into very small pieces, and as our guardians have\ntheir own business already, which is the care of freedom, they will\nhave enough to do without imitating. If they imitate they should\nimitate, not any meanness or baseness, but the good only; for the mask\nwhich the actor wears is apt to become his face. We cannot allow men to\nplay the parts of women, quarrelling, weeping, scolding, or boasting\nagainst the gods,—least of all when making love or in labour. They must\nnot represent slaves, or bullies, or cowards, drunkards, or madmen, or\nblacksmiths, or neighing horses, or bellowing bulls, or sounding\nrivers, or a raging sea. A good or wise man will be willing to perform\ngood and wise actions, but he will be ashamed to play an inferior part\nwhich he has never practised; and he will prefer to employ the\ndescriptive style with as little imitation as possible. The man who has\nno self-respect, on the contrary, will imitate anybody and anything;\nsounds of nature and cries of animals alike; his whole performance will\nbe imitation of gesture and voice. Now in the descriptive style there\nare few changes, but in the dramatic there are a great many. Poets and\nmusicians use either, or a compound of both, and this compound is very\nattractive to youth and their teachers as well as to the vulgar. But\nour State in which one man plays one part only is not adapted for\ncomplexity. And when one of these polyphonous pantomimic gentlemen\noffers to exhibit himself and his poetry we will show him every\nobservance of respect, but at the same time tell him that there is no\nroom for his kind in our State; we prefer the rough, honest poet, and\nwill not depart from our original models (Laws).\n\nNext as to the music. A song or ode has three parts,—the subject, the\nharmony, and the rhythm; of which the two last are dependent upon the\nfirst. As we banished strains of lamentation, so we may now banish the\nmixed Lydian harmonies, which are the harmonies of lamentation; and as\nour citizens are to be temperate, we may also banish convivial\nharmonies, such as the Ionian and pure Lydian. Two remain—the Dorian\nand Phrygian, the first for war, the second for peace; the one\nexpressive of courage, the other of obedience or instruction or\nreligious feeling. And as we reject varieties of harmony, we shall also\nreject the many-stringed, variously-shaped instruments which give\nutterance to them, and in particular the flute, which is more complex\nthan any of them. The lyre and the harp may be permitted in the town,\nand the Pan’s-pipe in the fields. Thus we have made a purgation of\nmusic, and will now make a purgation of metres. These should be like\nthe harmonies, simple and suitable to the occasion. There are four\nnotes of the tetrachord, and there are three ratios of metre, 3/2, 2/2,\n2/1, which have all their characteristics, and the feet have different\ncharacteristics as well as the rhythms. But about this you and I must\nask Damon, the great musician, who speaks, if I remember rightly, of a\nmartial measure as well as of dactylic, trochaic, and iambic rhythms,\nwhich he arranges so as to equalize the syllables with one another,\nassigning to each the proper quantity. We only venture to affirm the\ngeneral principle that the style is to conform to the subject and the\nmetre to the style; and that the simplicity and harmony of the soul\nshould be reflected in them all. This principle of simplicity has to be\nlearnt by every one in the days of his youth, and may be gathered\nanywhere, from the creative and constructive arts, as well as from the\nforms of plants and animals."
}

  "passage_text": "Other artists as well as poets should be warned against meanness or
unseemliness. Sculpture and painting equally with music must conform to
the law of simplicity. He who violates it cannot be allowed to work in
our city, and to corrupt the taste of our citizens. For our guardians
must grow up, not amid images of deformity which will gradually poison
and corrupt their souls, but in a land of health and beauty where they
will drink in from every object sweet and harmonious influences. And of
all these influences the greatest is the education given by music,
which finds a way into the innermost soul and imparts to it the sense
of beauty and of deformity. At first the effect is unconscious; but
when reason arrives, then he who has been thus trained welcomes her as
the friend whom he always knew. As in learning to read, first we
acquire the elements or letters separately, and afterwards their
combinations, and cannot recognize reflections of them until we know
the letters themselves;—in like manner we must first attain the
elements or essential forms of the virtues, and then trace their
combinations in life and experience. There is a music of the soul which
answers to the harmony of the world; and the fairest object of a
musical soul is the fair mind in the fair body. Some defect in the
latter may be excused, but not in the former. True love is the daughter
of temperance, and temperance is utterly opposed to the madness of
bodily pleasure. Enough has been said of music, which makes a fair
ending with love.

Next we pass on to gymnastics; about which I would remark, that the
soul is related to the body as a cause to an effect, and therefore if
we educate the mind we may leave the education of the body in her
charge, and need only give a general outline of the course to be
pursued. In the first place the guardians must abstain from strong
drink, for they should be the last persons to lose their wits. Whether
the habits of the palaestra are suitable to them is more doubtful, for
the ordinary gymnastic is a sleepy sort of thing, and if left off
suddenly is apt to endanger health. But our warrior athletes must be
wide-awake dogs, and must also be inured to all changes of food and
climate. Hence they will require a simpler kind of gymnastic, akin to
their simple music; and for their diet a rule may be found in Homer,
who feeds his heroes on roast meat only, and gives them no fish
although they are living at the sea-side, nor boiled meats which
involve an apparatus of pots and pans; and, if I am not mistaken, he
nowhere mentions sweet sauces. Sicilian cookery and Attic confections
and Corinthian courtezans, which are to gymnastic what Lydian and
Ionian melodies are to music, must be forbidden. Where gluttony and
intemperance prevail the town quickly fills with doctors and pleaders;
and law and medicine give themselves airs as soon as the freemen of a
State take an interest in them. But what can show a more disgraceful
state of education than to have to go abroad for justice because you
have none of your own at home? And yet there IS a worse stage of the
same disease—when men have learned to take a pleasure and pride in the
twists and turns of the law; not considering how much better it would
be for them so to order their lives as to have no need of a nodding
justice. And there is a like disgrace in employing a physician, not for
the cure of wounds or epidemic disorders, but because a man has by
laziness and luxury contracted diseases which were unknown in the days
of Asclepius. How simple is the Homeric practice of medicine. Eurypylus
after he has been wounded drinks a posset of Pramnian wine, which is of
a heating nature; and yet the sons of Asclepius blame neither the
damsel who gives him the drink, nor Patroclus who is attending on him.
The truth is that this modern system of nursing diseases was introduced
by Herodicus the trainer; who, being of a sickly constitution, by a
compound of training and medicine tortured first himself and then a
good many other people, and lived a great deal longer than he had any
right. But Asclepius would not practise this art, because he knew that
the citizens of a well-ordered State have no leisure to be ill, and
therefore he adopted the ‘kill or cure’ method, which artisans and
labourers employ. ‘They must be at their business,’ they say, ‘and have
no time for coddling: if they recover, well; if they don’t, there is an
end of them.’ Whereas the rich man is supposed to be a gentleman who
can afford to be ill. Do you know a maxim of Phocylides—that ‘when a
man begins to be rich’ (or, perhaps, a little sooner) ‘he should
practise virtue’? But how can excessive care of health be inconsistent
with an ordinary occupation, and yet consistent with that practice of
virtue which Phocylides inculcates? When a student imagines that
philosophy gives him a headache, he never does anything; he is always
unwell. This was the reason why Asclepius and his sons practised no
such art. They were acting in the interest of the public, and did not
wish to preserve useless lives, or raise up a puny offspring to
wretched sires. Honest diseases they honestly cured; and if a man was
wounded, they applied the proper remedies, and then let him eat and
drink what he liked. But they declined to treat intemperate and
worthless subjects, even though they might have made large fortunes out
of them. As to the story of Pindar, that Asclepius was slain by a
thunderbolt for restoring a rich man to life, that is a lie—following
our old rule we must say either that he did not take bribes, or that he
was not the son of a god."
